scenes.heading: Airflow Basics
scenes.narration: Apache Airflow orchestrates workflows as code, scheduling and monitoring pipelines defined in Python.

scenes.heading: Core Airflow concepts
bullets: DAGs: the workflow defined as a graph of tasks.
Operators: the units of work each task runs.
Scheduler: decides when tasks should run.
Executor and workers: actually run the tasks.
scenes.narration: In Airflow a DAG describes what work happens and in what order, all written in Python. Operators define the individual tasks, from running SQL to calling an API. The scheduler figures out when tasks are due, and the executor dispatches them to workers that do the running.

scenes.heading: How a run happens
steps: Creates a DAG run at schedule time
scenes.narration: The scheduler continuously reads your DAG files and, when a schedule fires, creates a DAG run. It queues tasks whose dependencies are met, and the executor hands them to workers. As each task succeeds or fails, its state updates and unblocks whatever comes next.

scenes.heading: A minimal DAG
scenes.code:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
import pendulum

with DAG(
    dag_id="daily_etl",
    schedule="0 6 * * *",
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2024, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
) as dag:
    extract = PythonOperator(task_id="extract", python_callable=run_extract)
    load    = PythonOperator(task_id="load",    python_callable=run_load)
    extract >> load
scenes.narration: This DAG runs every morning at six, defined entirely in Python. Two tasks wrap Python functions, and the shift operator declares that load depends on extract. Setting catchup to false tells Airflow not to backfill every missed day since the start date.

scenes.text: Airflow expresses pipelines as code using DAGs, operators, a scheduler, and workers, giving you version-controlled, observable orchestration.
scenes.narration: Because your workflows are just Python, they can be reviewed, tested, and versioned like any other software.
